samples.text:
In recent years, the idea of a four-day working week has become very popular. Some people think that the law should make all employers to give their workers a four-day week with the same salary. I partly agree with this idea.

On the one hand, a four-day week has many advantages for workers. People today are very stressed because they work long hours and they don't have enough time for their family and hobbies. With an extra day off, they can rest, do sport and spend time with their children. As a result, they will be more happy and healthy. Also, some companies which tried this system found that their employees worked more efficient and made less mistakes, so the productivity did not go down.

On the other hand, I don't think this should be a law for every employer. Some businesses cannot close one day in the week. For example, hospitals, restaurants and shops need workers every day. If they must give a four-day week without reducing pay, they have to hire more staff, and this is very expensive. Small companies especially may not have enough money and some of them can go bankrupt. Then the workers will lose their jobs, which is worse than working five days.

In my opinion, the government should encourage the companies to try the four-day week, for example by giving them some help or tax reduction, but it should not force them. Each company know its own situation better than the government.

In conclusion, I believe a four-day week can be good for employees, but it should not be required by law for all employers, because some businesses cannot afford it.

samples.text:
The four-day working week has attracted growing interest, and some people now argue that employers should be legally obliged to offer it without any cut in pay. Although I believe shorter working weeks can bring real benefits, I disagree that they should be imposed on all employers by law.

There is no doubt that a four-day week could improve employees' wellbeing. Many workers suffer from stress and exhaustion, and an extra day off would give them more time to rest, look after their families and pursue personal interests. Several companies that have experimented with the model report that staff became more focused and motivated, and that productivity stayed the same or even improved. A healthier and more satisfied workforce may also mean fewer sick days and lower staff turnover.

However, making this a legal requirement would ignore the huge differences between sectors. In offices where work can be reorganised, a four-day week may be relatively easy to introduce. But in hospitals, care homes, factories and shops, where services must be provided every day, reducing hours without cutting pay would mean hiring extra staff at considerable cost. Small businesses, which often operate on narrow profit margins, could struggle to survive, and some might respond by cutting jobs or raising prices.

A more practical solution would be for governments to encourage rather than force the change. They could support pilot schemes, share results with employers and perhaps give staff a legal right to request shorter hours, while leaving each organisation to decide what are workable.

In conclusion, a four-day week without loss of pay has clear advantages for employees, but a universal legal requirement would place an unfair burden on many businesses. Voluntary adoption, supported by government, is a more realistic way forward.
samples.why: Clear position maintained · ideas extended and supported, with some generalisation · logical organisation · good range of cohesive devices · some less common vocabulary and collocation · mostly error-free with one agreement slip.

samples.text:
Trials of the four-day week in various countries have produced encouraging results, prompting calls for employers to be legally required to offer it with no reduction in pay. While I am broadly sympathetic to the aims of this proposal, I disagree that it should be made compulsory, since a universal mandate would fail to account for the diversity of modern workplaces.

The potential benefits are considerable. Long working hours are associated with stress, burnout and poorer physical health, and an additional day of rest could allow employees to recover, care for relatives and engage more fully in family and community life. Many organisations that have adopted a shorter week report that staff concentrate more effectively, waste less time in unnecessary meetings and are less likely to leave, suggesting that output need not fall when hours do. For knowledge-based work in particular, time spent at a desk is a poor measure of productivity.

However, these results come largely from firms that chose to participate and were able to reorganise their work accordingly. The picture is very different in sectors where output is tied directly to hours, such as healthcare, retail, hospitality and manufacturing. A hospital cannot simply provide twenty per cent less care; to maintain services on full pay, it would need to recruit additional staff, often in areas already facing shortages. For small businesses with tight margins, the added cost could lead to redundancies or closure, ultimately harming the workers the policy is meant to help.

A more effective approach would be to promote the four-day week through incentives and evidence rather than compulsion. Governments could fund pilot programmes, publish their findings and give employees a statutory right to request flexible arrangements, which employers could refuse only on reasonable grounds.

In conclusion, a four-day week may well represent the future of work in many industries, but legislating it for every employer would be premature and potentially damaging.
